claims.text: In-situ aberration-corrected TEM equipped with a heating stage can reveal atomic-scale structural changes in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles during heating.
Such observations would experimentally validate predicted enhanced thermal stability in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Such observations would validate thermodynamically driven structural evolution under high-temperature conditions.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The initial nanoparticles have a theoretically predicted disordered multimetal arrangement.
The disordered multimetal arrangement has not yet been experimentally verified.
The nanoparticles will be subjected to controlled high-temperature conditions using a heating stage in an in-situ AC-TEM setup.
Real-time atomic-scale imaging during temperature ramping can reveal local ordering, diffusion, or segregation.
Direct in-situ imaging can link structural evolution at elevated temperatures to thermodynamic contributions.
Thermodynamic contributions may produce phase changes or enhanced structural stability.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will maintain a stable, disordered multimetal state up to a critical temperature.
Above the critical temperature, subtle atomic rearrangements or phase segregation will occur.
The high-temperature rearrangements or segregation will be consistent with thermodynamic predictions.
AC-TEM may fail to resolve ultrafast transient events or structural variations below its detection limits.
Beam-induced effects may mask structural variations observed during in-situ heating.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field says the disordered arrangement has not been experimentally verified, whereas the baseline treats a disordered room-temperature state as established rather than as a structure that must first be measured.
